lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- The First Forty-Eight Hours
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mauricio | Lesson 12 -- The First Forty-Eight Hours

listenings.text: Hi everyone, and welcome. A few practical things before tonight. The welcome dinner starts at seven, and it is not optional. If you are tired, come anyway and leave early. Nobody will notice when you leave, but everybody will notice if you are not there. Tomorrow, orientation starts at eight thirty in the main hall. If you are late, do not walk to the front. Sit in the back, and we will find you at the break. Your study group is on the back of your name tag. If you lose the tag, the front desk will print a new one. And one more thing. If you have a question, ask it. This week is expensive, and the questions are the cheapest part of it.

The first time a professor cold called me, I was sure my English would fail. She said my name and asked one question: would you sell the company? I had two seconds. I said, no, because the market will recover next year. That was it. One sentence and one reason. Here is what I learned that morning. If you try to give a perfect answer, you will freeze. If you give a short answer, the professor will ask a follow-up question, and then you are in a conversation, not in an exam. On Monday I was afraid of the cold call. By Wednesday I wanted it. By Friday I was raising my hand.

paras: Most people arrive on Sunday afternoon with jet lag and a bag of pre-reading that they did not finish. If you arrive early, you will have time to sleep before the orientation on Monday morning. If you arrive late, you will meet your cohort for the first time while you are tired, and first impressions last all week.

At the orientation, you will get a name tag and an assigned study group of six people. Your group will stay the same for the whole program. If you forget someone's name on day two, ask again. Nobody will mind on Tuesday. On Friday, it will be harder.

The part that worries most people is the cold call. In many sessions, the professor will ask someone a question without warning. If the professor cold calls you, you will have a few seconds, not a few minutes. Do not wing it, and do not apologize. Say what you think in one sentence, then give one reason.

A last piece of advice from past participants: prepare three answers before you arrive. Who are you? What does your company do? What do you want to take home? If someone puts you on the spot, you will not need to invent anything. You will only need to remember.
